newsitem.title: FRANCE: Stock rally encourages French firms to shed stakes.
newsitem.headline: Stock rally encourages French firms to shed stakes.

text.p: French companies are taking advantage of a big stockmarket rally to shed stakes in unrelated businesses, streamlining their portfolios and generating rich capital gains.

"There is an underlying trend of selling peripheral businesses and focusing on core activities, and the opportunity is offered now by the level of the market," said equities analyst Gary Dugan at J.P. Morgan Securities Ltd.

"There's good profits to be taken," he added. The bourse's blue chip CAC-40 index, which rose 27 percent last year, has advanced a further 13 percent since the beginning of 1997 to touch a historic high on Friday at 2,643.98 points.
Among the recent divestments, Compagnie de Suez is selling control of salt company Cie des Salins du Midi et des Salines de l'Est as well as its half stake in Facto Holdings.
Fund managers say Suez is also preparing to sell its interest of around nine percent in French hotel group Accor held by its Societe Generale de Belgique subsidiary.
Financial group Paribas sold nearly two million shares last week in Elf Aquitaine, the last bit of a stake acquired during Elf's privatisation in 1993.
"Paribas's strategy is to invest in small and medium-sized companies with growth potential rather than hold big industrial holdings," an official at the company said.
Tyremaker Michelin sold 2.6 percent of PSA Peugeot Citroen in December, or nearly half its stake in the car company.

Axa-UAP, the world's second-largest insurer formed by the merger of Axa and UAP, sold part of its stakes in Banque Nationale de Paris and Suez last month and pulled out completely from retailer Galeries Lafayette.

Axa chairman Claude Bebear said he would not divest holdings in a way that risked destabilising the companies in which it held the stakes. But he said Axa had no intention of being a "godfather of the French economy".
Axa had previously sold its stake in bank Societe Generale as part of Societe Generale chairman Marc Vienot's drive to eliminate cross-shareholdings in French corporations.
A 1995 report on corporate governance drafted by a committee chaired by Vienot recommended eliminating these cross-holdings which it said encouraged "reciprocal complacency".

The cross-holdings, which have been heavily criticised by foreign investors who account for around half of the trading activity in France, were arranged partly to forge defensive alliances among newly-listed companies and also to compensate for a dearth in capital invested in French equities.
The government is trying to redirect capital flows through the establishment, proposed in a bill, of private pension funds. The funds are expected to start operating in 1998.
A study by consulting firm Vuchot Ward Howell issued in December said very few cross-holdings had been dismantled since the Vienot report was issued.

The exceptions are Societe Generale, which sold its interest in chemicals group Rhone-Poulenc as well as its Axa stake, and Lyonnaise des Eaux and oil company Total, which eliminated their cross-holdings last year.

"I think people are waiting to see private pension funds put in place before they do something about cross-shareholdings," said Olivier Blitz at Paris brokerage IFF. He said recent divestment moves tended to be associated with restructurings.

The Organisation for Economic Cooperation and Development has welcomed the establishment in France of private pension funds. The rates of return on equity at French companies were lowest among those that had cross-holdings which eased "pressures to maximise performance", said the OECD.

"If funds would rise to a certain importance -- this is not certain, as pension coverage by the pay-as-you-go system is high -- and if funds were independent from listed companies and their shareholders, the new funds would contribute to changing the corporate governance landscape," the OECD said.
